ateret-zekenim/1:_: That the candles should not go out — written in Hagahot Chadashim to Rif: even on weekdays if he kindled before wind and it went out he must return and kindle where wind is not common, since they cannot stand before wind it is as if he did not give the measure of oil — end; Or Zaru'a wrote similarly one should not wedge candles close to each other until they heat and fall — same reason.
kaf-hachayyim/2:_: (ב) There. One must place something outside, etc., for a candle behind the door — forbidden to open and close against it. Tur. See above siman 677 seif 1 whether there is a difference if candles are fixed in the wall directly opposite the door — door west, candles east — versus fixed in the wall behind the door — see there and in our words there.
levushei-serad/1:_: {Rama: Shulchan Aruch seif 2} On the door itself, etc. — when opening the door he brings oil closer to the candle or distances it and it is kindling or extinguishing; the reason for permission — see Tur and siman 677 seif 1 regarding unspecified prohibition — end.
peri-megadim/1:_: What the Mechaber wrote regarding the door itself — forbidden means with oil that brings closer and distances and is extinguishing and kindling, not with wax; see siman 677 and Levush here that the door's base is not a base since the door serves the house and is as attached. Some are lenient even with oil — see Tur, Rabbi Meir of Rothenburg z"l in the name of his teacher R' Shmuel; one may say why did the Mechaber not bring in siman 677? Some permit; one may say with strain that for Hanukkah one may say psik reisha he does not want to kindle the oil quickly; for all Hanukkah lights one must kindle half an hour and puts oil sparingly — in the case of wicks and oils, etc., Hanukkah speaks for the view permitted after burning; like oil burning terumah one must burn and it was mentioned in Mishnah — even so they kindle Hanukkah giving sparse measure; also distancing and extinguishing he does not want on Hanukkah — therefore here some permit; see Levush here.
